title: 20C3M: CMIP collecting data from 20th century coupled model simulations

venue.name: Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel (GEOMAR)

problem: Robustly assessing 20th-century climate change is hindered by model and forcing uncertainties because the lack of a centralized simulation database from different research groups prevents the comprehensive multi-model comparisons needed to quantify these uncertainties and attribute causes.
method: The paper proposes the "20th Century Climate in Coupled Models" (20C3M) pilot project to collect and archive a standardized subset of data from various 20th-century climate model simulations to facilitate multi-model comparisons, attribution studies, and assessments of past and future climate change.
task: The task is to collect and archive a standardized set of output data from various modeling groups' simulations of the 20th-century climate under the "20th Century Climate in Coupled Models" (20C3M) pilot project to facilitate climate change research.
innovation: This paper announces the "20th Century Climate in Coupled Models" (20C3M) project, a CMIP initiative to collect and archive 20th-century simulation data from multiple models, creating a database to facilitate research on climate change detection, attribution, and model uncertainty.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: Therefore, it was decided at the recent meeting of the Working Group on Coupled Models (WGCM, the parent committee of Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP)), to go forward with a new CMIP pilot project called "20th Century Climate in Coupled Models" (20C3M). The goal is to collect data from 20th century simulations from as many coupled ocean-atmosphere models as possible. The accessibility of the data to the user community will help in providing assessments of past and future climate change by a variety of methods, incorporating forcing and model uncertainty.

Many modelling groups have completed or are in the process of performing simulations of the 20th century with ocean-atmosphere general circulation models. The simulations are driven with various combinations of external climate forcings, such as anthropogenic increases in greenhouse gases and sulphate aerosols, changes in solar radiation and forcing by explosive volcanism; and the different forcings are incorporated either into separate simulations or combined.
